rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 60 (Legge, SBE 39, ch. 60)
rows.original: 非其神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人
rows.translation: James Legge, The Tao Teh King, SBE 39 (1891)
rows.says: When the world is ruled by the Tao, the spirits do not harm people, and neither does the sage. Neither side harms the other. It describes good rule rather than giving an order.
rows.bearing: A wider duty not to harm people (rule 7). It reaches everyone, with no in-group limit, so it includes K1 and K0 (whoever harms no one kills no one). Borderline: it describes the sage, here as ruler, and does not name killing or private persons. Same basis as Article I row 7b and the households annex (L1, taught, borderline). Read with rows for chapters 81, 49, 27 and 62.
rows.strength: Clear teaching, borderline (wider rule; addressed to the sage-ruler)

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 81 (closing lines)
rows.original: 天之道，利而不害；聖人之道，為而不爭
rows.translation: F. H. Balfour, Taoist Texts (1894), as hosted on sacred-texts.com; Legge (1891) for comparison (Legge reads 利 as the 'sharpness' of Heaven's Way, from memory, not checked)
rows.says: The Way of Heaven benefits and does not harm; the way of the sage is to act without contending. Heaven's Way is the model the sage follows.
rows.bearing: A wider rule of non-harm that is not limited to rulers (rule 7): it states the pattern every follower of the Tao should copy. It reaches all beings, so it includes K1 and K0. Borderline because it describes Heaven's Way rather than commanding, and because Legge's reading of 利 differs (either reading keeps 'does not harm').
rows.strength: Clear teaching, borderline (wider rule; read with ch. 60)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): sacred-texts.com Taoist Texts page gives ch. 81 as 'the TAO of Heaven confers benefit, and injures not' (translator shown by page, Balfour). rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 49 (received text; the Mawangdui manuscript reads 聖人恆無心)
rows.original: 善者，吾善之；不善者，吾亦善之
rows.says: The sage takes the people's hearts as his own. He is good to the good, and good to those who are not good as well.
rows.bearing: Shows the reach of the wider duty: it covers 'the not-good', so it protects 'the wicked' as K1 requires (rule 7). It does not name killing, so on its own it is Implied for K1; read with ch. 60 it is part of the Clear teaching, borderline (as in Article I row 7a).
rows.strength: Clear teaching, borderline (for the reach of the duty; read with ch. 60)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in earlier project research (Article I, row 7a): ctext.org ch. 49 with Legge. Not re-searched in this run.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 27
rows.original: 聖人常善救人，故無棄人
rows.says: The sage is always good at saving people, so he casts away no one. The same chapter calls the good person the teacher of the not-good, and the not-good person the material of the good.
rows.bearing: Universal care that excludes no one, including the not-good. Supports the reach of K1 (everyone, 'the wicked' included). It does not name killing, so for K1 and K0 it supports the wider rule rather than standing alone (rule 7).
rows.strength: Implied alone; part of the Clear teaching, borderline, when read with ch. 60

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 62
rows.original: 人之不善，何棄之有
rows.says: The Tao is the treasure of the good and the protection of the not-good. Even people who are not good are not abandoned by it. (The chapter's later line that by the Tao 'the guilty may escape' was not checked in this run.)
rows.bearing: Supports the reach of K1: the not-good are not to be cast off (rule 7, reach). It does not name killing; Implied for K1 and K0 on its own.
rows.strength: Implied alone (reach of the wider rule)

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 74
rows.original: 常有司殺者殺。夫代司殺者殺，是謂代大匠斲
rows.says: Threatening death is useless if people do not fear it. If they did, and wrongdoers could be seized and put to death, who would dare? But there is always One who presides over killing; whoever kills in his place is like someone hewing wood in place of a master carpenter, and seldom escapes cutting his own hands.
rows.bearing: About a ruler's capital punishment, so context only (rule 5). It both presupposes judicial killing (the conditional) and warns rulers against taking killing into their own hands. By argument a fortiori it reaches private killing (if even a ruler must not kill in Heaven's place, a private person may not), but that is not what the text plainly says: Implied for K1. It permits no private killing, so it does not contradict (rule 2).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): sacred-texts.com SBE 39 ch. 74 page with Legge's text and his note that the chapter 'sets forth the inefficiency of capital punishment, and warns rulers against the infliction of it'.

rows.original: 司殺者 (read as 天, Heaven)
rows.translation: James Legge's English summary of Heshang Gong (1891)
rows.says: Heshang Gong identifies the One who presides over killing as Heaven, which dwells on high, rules all below and takes note of people's wrongdoing.
rows.bearing: The tradition's own classical reading: the right to take life belongs to Heaven, and any human who kills in Heaven's place usurps it. This strengthens the reading of ch. 74 against killing on one's own authority, but as a commentary it cannot decide a label (rule 1).

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 31
rows.original: 夫樂殺人者，則不可以得志於天下矣；殺人之眾，以哀悲泣之，戰勝以喪禮處之
rows.says: Weapons are instruments of ill omen, used only when there is no choice. To praise victory is to delight in killing people, and whoever delights in killing people cannot have his way in the world. Those who have killed many should weep for them in grief, and a victory is treated with the rites of mourning.
rows.bearing: War is context only (rule 5). For K3 it limits all killing in war (only when unavoidable, with grief, never with delight) but does not single out people who are not fighting, so Implied for K3. For K1 and K0 it shows the tradition treats killing people as an evil to be mourned even when unavoidable (Implied). Its condemnation of 'delight in killing' also bears on K0's 'hatred', but within war.
rows.strength: n/a (context); Implied for K3 and K1

support.reconciliation: No counted text (Tao Te Ching or Zhuangzi) was found that permits, commands or approves a private person, master, parent, husband or crowd killing anyone, so there is no contradicting counted text to reconcile. The hard texts are of three kinds, and the tradition handles each in its own terms. (1) Judicial killing. Tao Te Ching 74 (Tier 1, all branches, verified) presupposes that rulers execute wrongdoers but warns that whoever kills in the place of 'the One who presides over killing' cuts his own hands. Heshang Gong, the classical commentary that corpus.md names for reconciliation (Tier 2, transmitted within religious Taoism, standing: standard traditional reading, not counted), reads that One as Heaven, so the right to take life belongs to Heaven and humans who take it on their own authority usurp it; Legge's note says the chapter warns rulers against capital punishment. Zhuangzi 6's True Man who is 'lenient in putting people to death' (Inner Chapters, unverified) would temper, not extend, state killing. Both are context only (rule 5). (2) War. Tao Te Ching 31 (Tier 1, verified) reconciles itself: weapons are used only when unavoidable, victory is not praised, and the many killed are mourned with funeral rites. Context only for K1 and K0; Implied support for K3. (3) Apparent indifference. Tao Te Ching 5 (straw dogs) is read by the classical commentators (Wang Bi; attribution reported in earlier project research, not confirmed) as impartiality and non-interference, and the same book says the sage harms no one (60) and casts away no one, the not-good included (27, 49, 62). Zhuangzi's stories of robbers and his calm acceptance of death report or reflect on killing and death without approving any killing (rule 4); Guo Xiang's commentary was not checked. Later Taoist texts make the line explicit: the Ganying Pian (Tier 2, a 12th-century morality book in the Daozang, not counted) lists killing people for their wealth, wrongful killing, and killing those who have surrendered among wicked deeds that bring retribution, and says even insects and plants must not be harmed; the religious branches' precept texts are reported to place 'do not kill' first (Lingbao Ten Precepts; Hundred and Eighty Precepts), but these were not verified. No modern Taoist body's statement was searched.

K1.label: Not contradicted, taught (borderline), through a wider rule
K1.reason: Tao Te Ching 60 (the sage harms no one), read with 81 (Heaven's Way benefits and does not harm), 49, 27 and 62 (no one, not even the not-good, is cast away), teaches a wider duty not to harm that reaches every person, 'the wicked' included (rule 7). This is the same basis on which Article I and its households annex counted Taoism. Borderline because no counted text names killing by private persons; the lines describe the sage (often as ruler) and Heaven's Way rather than giving rules; and Legge's reading of 利 in ch. 81 differs. No counted text permits a private killing: Tao Te Ching 74 and Zhuangzi 6 (judicial) and Tao Te Ching 31 (war) are context only (rule 5), and Zhuangzi's stories are reporting, not approval (rule 4). If a reviewer holds that the sage-ruler's non-harm does not bind private persons, the label falls to Silent (rule 8), not Contradicted. Newborns are covered only through the general word 'people' (rule 9); no counted text speaks of them specifically. The Ganying Pian's explicit lines are Tier 2 and do not decide (rule 1).

K0.label: Not contradicted, taught (borderline)
K0.reason: K0 is narrower than K1, so the same wider rule (Tao Te Ching 60 with 81, 49, 27, 62) covers it (rule 7), with the same borderline caveat. Tao Te Ching 63 (repay injury with kindness) adds Clear teaching against revenge, though not naming killing. The 'gain' and 'anger' clauses rest on the wider rule; Tao Te Ching 68 ('the best fighter shows no anger') and 46 ('no fault greater than the wish to get') are unverified leads that could strengthen them. Zhuangzi 28 (lives outweigh land) bears on 'gain' but is a ruler's choice in war (context, Implied). The Ganying Pian is Explicit against killing for wealth but is Tier 2 and does not decide (rule 1). No counted text permits killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge.

K3.label: Not contradicted, silent in counted texts (Implied support only)
K3.reason: Tao Te Ching 31 (verified) limits all killing in war: only when unavoidable, without delight, mourned with funeral rites. It does not single out children, the old, civilians or the surrendered, so it is Implied for K3, not Clear teaching. Tao Te Ching 30 and 69 are unverified leads of the same kind. No counted text approves killing non-combatants. The Ganying Pian (Tier 2, not counted) is Explicit against slaying those who have surrendered, which would be K3 taught in part if it counted.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 5 (received text)
rows.original: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗
rows.says: Heaven and Earth are 'not benevolent' and treat all things as straw dogs; the sage is 'not benevolent' and treats the people as straw dogs. Straw dogs were ritual figures honoured during a sacrifice and thrown away after it.
rows.bearing: An image about impartiality. It says nothing about killing or about what one person may do to another. Rule 4: Implied; does not decide K1, K0 or K3. Its apparent force depends on translation ('impartial' in Legge, 'ruthless' in some modern versions; translations.md). Read with chapters 27, 49 and 60 of the same book (rows below).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's Article I research: ctext.org Dao De Jing page with the chapter 5 Chinese. Two further searches in this pass for Heshang Gong's comment did not display it.

rows.tier: 2 (classical commentary, used for reconciliation; not counted)
rows.branch: all branches (Heshang Gong's commentary is transmitted within religious Taoism; Wang Bi's is the standard literati reading)
rows.reference: Heshang Gong, Laozi zhangju, ch. 5; Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, ch. 5
rows.original: 天地任自然，無為無造 (Wang Bi); 不以仁恩，任自然也 (Heshang Gong, lead)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Both read 不仁 as letting things follow their own course without personal favour, not as cruelty. Wang Bi: Heaven and Earth do not make grass for beasts, yet beasts eat grass, and do not make dogs for people, yet people eat dogs; they act without contrivance. Heshang Gong: Heaven and Earth, and the sage who models himself on them, act by spontaneity rather than by handing out favours.
rows.bearing: The tradition's own classical reading narrows chapter 5 to impartiality and non-interference, which removes any reading of it as licence to harm people. Reconciliation only (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: Wang Bi's opening clause appeared in this pass only in an unattributed quotation in a teaching document (rong0922.url.tw), not on a project reference site; Heshang Gong's wording was not displayed. Article I reports the same reading from R. Wagner, A Chinese Reading of the Daodejing (2003), a book not checked online.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 27
rows.original: 是以聖人常善救人，故無棄人
rows.says: The sage is always skilful at saving people, and so casts away no one; he does the same for things.
rows.bearing: The same book's answer to chapter 5: no one is discarded. For K1 and K0 it is a wider rule that reaches everyone (rule 7), taught through the sage's example: Clear teaching, borderline, because it describes the sage (often the ruler) rather than stating a rule for everyone. Against any grading of protection by status.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's Article I research: ctext.org 'Dao De Jing : 27' showed this line; Legge's English confirmed on sacred-texts.com.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 49 (received text; the Mawangdui manuscript reads 聖人恆無心)
rows.original: 善者，吾善之；不善者，吾亦善之 ... 聖人皆孩之
rows.says: The sage has no fixed mind and takes the people's mind as his own. He is good to the good and good also to the not-good; in Legge's reading he deals with them all as his children.
rows.bearing: Care reaches the not-good, so no counted text limits protection to the good or to one's own group. Wider rule for K1 and K0 (rule 7): Clear teaching, borderline (addressed to the sage-ruler; some translators read 皆孩之 as making people childlike).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's Article I research: ctext.org 'Dao De Jing : 49' with Legge's English; also classics.mit.edu.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 60
rows.original: 非其神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人
rows.says: Ruling a large state is like cooking small fish. When the world is ruled by the Tao, the spirits of the dead do not harm people, and neither does the sage.
rows.bearing: A wider rule (the sage harms no one) that includes not killing (rule 7). It describes good rule rather than giving an order, so it is Clear teaching, borderline.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's Article I research on sacred-texts.com (Legge, SBE 39). The households research could confirm it only on a site not on the project's list, so a re-check on ctext is still pending.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 62
rows.original: 人之不善，何棄之有
rows.says: Lead from memory: even if a person is not good, why should they be cast away?
rows.bearing: If confirmed, it extends the sage's care expressly to wrongdoers. That would answer any reading in which 'the wicked' lose protection. Unverified, so it does not decide (rule 1).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched; the shared search limit was reached.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 63 (received Heshang Gong and Wang Bi texts)
rows.original: 報怨以德
rows.says: Among sayings on acting without striving: recompense injury with kindness. Legge notes that the chapter describes the way of the Tao rather than giving an order.
rows.bearing: K0: answering injury with kindness rules out killing from revenge or resentment. Clear teaching. A modern conjecture (Yan Lingfeng, followed by Chen Guying; unverified) moves the phrase to chapter 79, where it might be read as questioned. The received texts of both classical commentators keep it in chapter 63. Even on the conjecture, chapter 79's alternative is a sage who presses no claims on others, not revenge.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (for K0; placement disputed by a modern conjecture)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's Article I research: sacred-texts.com, Legge chapter 63.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 74
rows.original: 若使民常畏死，而為奇者，吾得執而殺之，孰敢？常有司殺者殺。夫代司殺者殺，是謂代大匠斲
rows.says: If the people always feared death, and those who act perversely (為奇者) could always be seized and put to death, who would dare? There is always one who presides over killing. Whoever kills in his place is like someone hewing wood in place of the master carpenter, and seldom escapes cutting his own hands.
rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5): it assumes a ruler's power to execute. It also warns that whoever takes killing into his own hands harms himself. Commentators, Heshang Gong among them, read 司殺者 as Heaven (lead from memory, unverified). If even the ruler is warned off, the chapter gives no warrant for a private person to kill. 為奇者 can be read politically ('deviants'), but that is a court matter.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search), but only on satyori.com, a site not on the project's list (households research, TA-5). Not re-searched in this pass; re-check on ctext.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 30 and 31
rows.original: 夫樂殺人者，則不可以得志於天下矣 ... 殺人之眾，以哀悲泣之；戰勝，以喪禮處之 (31); 善者果而已，不敢以取強 (30)
rows.says: Lead from memory. Chapter 31: weapons are instruments of ill omen, used by the superior man only when he cannot avoid it. Whoever delights in killing cannot get his will in the world. The many who are killed should be wept over, and a victory should be kept with the rites of mourning. Chapter 30: where armies have been, briars grow; a skilful commander achieves his aim and stops, and does not use force to show his strength.
rows.bearing: K3 context: restraint in war and mourning for the slain, but no line names non-combatants, children or those who surrender. Implied for K3. If confirmed, chapter 31 is Clear teaching against delighting in killing (K0). Unverified, so it does not decide (rule 1).
rows.strength: Implied (K3); Clear teaching for K0 if confirmed
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched in this pass (shared search limit reached); listed as unverified in the households research.

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 19, Da Sheng 達生 ('The Full Understanding of Life'), dialogue of Liezi and Guan Yin 關尹
rows.original: 復讎者不折鏌、干，雖有忮心者不怨飄瓦，是以天下平均
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project (Legge's English for this line not displayed)
rows.says: Someone taking revenge does not break the swords Moye and Ganjiang (only the killer is blamed), and even a resentful man does not blame a tile the wind blows down; so the world stays even. In Guan Yin's account of the perfect man whom nothing can harm, the point is that blame falls on agents with intent, not on things.
rows.bearing: It presupposes blood revenge (復讎) as a known practice and uses it as an image. It neither approves nor condemns revenge. Rule 4: Implied; does not decide K0 or K1.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): ctext.org, the search result for the Da Sheng chapter page displayed this Chinese line; Legge's English was not displayed.

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 25, Ze Yang 則陽, King Ying of Wei and the Marquis of Tian (snail's horns parable)
rows.original: 魏瑩怒，將使人刺之 ... 以匹夫從讎
rows.translation: James Legge (1891) for the first line; the rest paraphrased by the project
rows.says: King Ying of Wei, angry that the Marquis of Tian (Qi) broke a treaty, means to send a man to assassinate him. His general Xishou says it is shameful for a ruler of ten thousand chariots to take revenge like a common man (匹夫從讎) and offers to lead 200,000 soldiers instead. Jizi opposes war; Huazi says that those who urge war and those who urge peace both confuse the state. Dai Jinren then tells of two kingdoms on a snail's two horns whose war leaves tens of thousands dead, and the king's anger subsides.
rows.bearing: A ruler's order against another state: context only (rule 5; exclusions a and b). The chapter approves neither the assassination nor the war, and the parable mocks both. Private revenge is spoken of as the conduct of a common man, not as a right. Implied; does not decide.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in part: ctext.org Ze Yang page, Legge: 'The king was enraged, and intended to send a man to assassinate him'. The 匹夫從讎 line and the snail parable were seen only on a personal blog (udn.com), not on a project site.

rows.branch: all branches (in Guo Xiang's 33-chapter text and the Daozang)
rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 29, Dao Zhi 盜跖 ('Robber Zhi')
rows.original: 膾人肝而餔之
rows.says: Lead from memory: Robber Zhi leads 9,000 men, raids states and kills, and eats minced human liver. Confucius goes to reform him and is routed in debate. Zhi says the sage-kings were the true source of killing (the Yellow Emperor fought Chiyou, Tang banished his lord, King Wu killed Zhou) and threatens to add Confucius's liver to his meal.
rows.bearing: The killings are reported, not approved. Zhi's speech is used to mock Confucian morality, not to justify his crimes, and nothing in the chapter calls his killing right. Rule 4: Implied; does not decide. Su Shi doubted the chapter (reconciliation row below).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched (shared search limit reached).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 10, Qu Qie 胠篋 ('Cutting Open Satchels'); with ch. 8, Pian Mu 駢拇
rows.original: 田成子一旦殺齊君而盜其國 ... 盜亦有道 (ch. 10); 伯夷死名於首陽之下，盜跖死利於東陵之上 (ch. 8)
rows.says: Lead from memory. Chapter 10: Tian Chengzi killed the ruler of Qi and stole his state, and because he also stole the sages' laws he kept it safely; robbers too have their 'way' (sageness, courage, righteousness, wisdom, kindness). Chapter 8: Bo Yi died for fame and Robber Zhi died for gain; both harmed their nature alike.
rows.bearing: Satire on how the sages' morality serves the strong. The killing of a ruler is reported, not approved, and chapter 8's point is self-harm, not the rightness of killing. Rule 4: Implied; does not decide.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched (shared search limit reached).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 2, Qi Wu Lun 齊物論 (perspectivism), with ch. 6, Da Zong Shi (forgetting both Yao and Jie)
rows.original: 彼亦一是非，此亦一是非 (ch. 2); 與其譽堯而非桀也，不如兩忘而化其道 (ch. 6)
rows.says: Lead in part from memory. Each standpoint has its own right and wrong (ch. 2). Rather than praise the good king Yao and condemn the tyrant Jie, it is better to forget both and be transformed in the Way (ch. 6).
rows.bearing: A general hard text: it can be read as dissolving moral judgment, including judgment of killers. It says nothing permitting killing. Rule 4: Implied; does not decide. The same Inner Chapters warn that whoever brings calamity on others will have calamity brought on him (ch. 4, 菑人者，人必反菑之; verified on ctext in Article I research), and Guo Xiang reads the perspectivism as each thing being content in its own nature (unverified).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: the ch. 2 page was located on ctext in Article I research, but the line was not displayed; ch. 6 not searched.

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 4, Ren Jian Shi 人間世, section 1 (Yan Hui and Confucius on the ruler of Wei)
rows.original: 輕用民死 ... 昔者桀殺關龍逢，紂殺王子比干
rows.says: Lead from memory: Confucius warns Yan Hui that the ruler of Wei spends his people's lives lightly and will kill him, as the tyrants Jie and Zhou killed the ministers Guan Longfeng and Prince Bi Gan who remonstrated with them.
rows.bearing: Rulers' killings, reported with disapproval: context only (rule 5). No approval of killing. Implied.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: the section was located on ctext in Article I research (for its 菑人 line), but these lines were not displayed.

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 6, Da Zong Shi 大宗師, the True Man of old (古之真人)
rows.original: 以刑為體 ... 以刑為體者，綽乎其殺也
rows.says: Lead from memory: the True Man of old takes punishment as the body of government, and is lenient (綽) in putting people to death.
rows.bearing: Accepts and tempers judicial punishment: context only (rule 5). Some editors are said to treat the passage as a later insertion because it sits oddly with the Inner Chapters (not checked).
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: the chapter was found on ctext in the households research (TA-6), but the passage was not displayed; not re-searched.

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 11, Zai You 在宥; ch. 25, Ze Yang 則陽 (Bo Ju weeps over an executed man)
rows.original: 今世殊死者相枕也，桁楊者相推也，刑戮者相望也 (ch. 11); 古之君人者，以得為在民，以失為在己 (ch. 25)
rows.says: Lead from memory. Chapter 11: today the executed lie pillowed on one another and the shackled jostle each other, and Confucians and Mohists strut among them. Chapter 25: Bo Ju weeps over the corpse of an executed criminal in Qi and says rulers of old credited success to the people and blamed failure on themselves, while rulers now create the conditions for crime and then punish it.
rows.bearing: Criticism of state punishment: context only (rule 5). It limits rather than widens killing. Implied.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched (shared search limit reached).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 24, Xu Wugui 徐無鬼
rows.original: 愛民，害民之始也；為義偃兵，造兵之本也 ... 殺人之士民，兼人之土地，以養吾私與吾神者，其戰不知孰善
rows.translation: Legge (1891) via ctext for the first line ('To love the people is the first step to injure them'); the rest paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Xu Wugui tells the Marquis of Wei that loving the people (as a policy) begins harming them, and that ending war for the sake of righteousness is the root of making war. Lead from memory: he adds that when one kills another state's officers and people and annexes its land to feed one's own desires, no one can say which side in such a war is good.
rows.bearing: K3 context: condemns wars of conquest and the killing of another state's soldiers and people, but sets no rule protecting non-combatants within a war. Implied for K3; does not decide. The 'love the people' line targets contrived benevolence, not care (Article I, section I).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in part: the 愛民 line on ctext.org in Article I research. The 殺人之士民 line is UNVERIFIED (the search for it was refused by the shared search limit).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 28, Rang Wang 讓王, Taiwang Danfu leaves Bin
rows.original: 不以所用養害所養
rows.says: Lead from memory: when the Di people attack, the ancestor of the Zhou, Taiwang Danfu, leaves his land rather than have his people killed defending it, saying one must not harm those one nourishes for the sake of what nourishes them (the land). The same chapter tells of men who drowned themselves rather than accept a throne.
rows.bearing: K3 context: a ruler refuses war to spare his people's lives. Implied for K3. The suicide stories fall under exclusion (d) and do not bear on K1.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched (shared search limit reached).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 30, Shuo Jian 說劍 ('Delight in the Sword-fight')
rows.says: King Wen of Zhao keeps thousands of swordsmen who fight before him day and night, and many die each year. Zhuangzi persuades him to give it up by describing the swords of the Son of Heaven, the feudal lord and the common man. Lead from memory: afterwards the swordsmen kill themselves where they live.
rows.bearing: A ruler's lethal sport, treated as ruinous and ended: Implied support, not counter. The swordsmen's deaths fall under exclusion (d). Su Shi doubted the chapter.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in part: ctext.org page for the chapter, showing the king testing his swordsmen before Zhuangzi performs. The death figures and the ending were not displayed.

rows.tier: outside the corpus (Song dynasty literati criticism)
rows.branch: philosophical readers chiefly; the chapters stay in Guo Xiang's text and the Daozang
rows.reference: Su Shi 蘇軾 (1037 to 1101), Zhuangzi citang ji 莊子祠堂記 ('Record of the Shrine Hall of Zhuangzi')
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Lead from memory: Su Shi argued that the Dao Zhi and Yu Fu chapters attack Confucius in earnest, unlike Zhuangzi's own veiled support of him, and that Rang Wang and Shuo Jian are shallow and do not reach the Way; he held all four to be later additions.
rows.bearing: The tradition's literati readers placed chapters 28 to 31 (Robber Zhi, the sword-fight, the suicides) below the rest of the book. Standing: an influential scholar's judgment, not a Taoist religious authority, and the chapters remain canonical in Guo Xiang's edition. Reconciliation only; it does not change a label, since nothing in those chapters approves killing anyway.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched (shared search limit reached).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 7, Ying Di Wang 應帝王, section 7 (Hundun)
rows.original: 日鑿一竅，七日而渾沌死
rows.says: Shu and Hu, wishing to repay Hundun's kindness, bore one opening into him each day so that he can see, hear, eat and breathe like them; on the seventh day he dies.
rows.bearing: An unintended, well-meant killing used as a parable against imposing on others: exclusion (f) and rule 4. It warns against harming others, so it does not cut against K1.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's Article I research: ctext.org, Ying Di Wang section 7.

rows.branch: religious Taoism (scripture since 742 as Chongxu zhenjing); philosophical readers often read it too
rows.reference: Liezi 列子 ch. 5, Tang Wen 湯問, customs of distant peoples (parallels: Mozi, Jie Zang; Bowuzhi as quoted in Taiping Guangji ch. 480)
rows.original: 其長子生，則鮮而食之，謂之宜弟 ... 上以為政，下以為俗，而未足為異也
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Lead from memory for the Liezi: east of Yue lives a people who cut up and eat their firstborn son, saying it is good for his younger brothers, and who abandon the grandmother when the grandfather dies. Other peoples' funeral customs follow. The rulers make these things policy and the people custom, so they are not to be thought strange. In the Bowuzhi version (quoted in the Taiping Guangji, which notes that it is also in Mozi) the close reads 未足為非, 'not to be thought wrong'. Mozi tells the same story to condemn taking habit for right (便其習而義其俗).
rows.bearing: It reports the killing of newborns among foreign peoples in order to show that customs differ. It neither commands nor commends the practice for anyone. Rule 4: Implied. Tier 2, flagged, not counted, and unverified in the Liezi: does not decide K1 (rule 1). It is the only text found in or near the Taoist corpus that mentions killing newborns without condemning it.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED for the Liezi: the passage was not displayed from the Liezi text. The parallel, with 未足為非, was seen in this pass on zh.wikisource (Taiping Guangji ch. 480, citing the Bowuzhi and Mozi).

rows.branch: religious Taoism; philosophical readers often read it too
rows.reference: Liezi ch. 5, Tang Wen 湯問, Lai Dan 來丹 and the sword Xiaolian 宵練
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Lead from memory: Lai Dan seeks to avenge his father, killed by Hei Luan. Kong Zhou lends him one of three ancient swords that cut without killing; Lai Dan strikes Hei Luan and his son, and they feel only slight discomfort.
rows.bearing: It reports an attempt at private revenge without approving it, and the story ensures the revenge fails. Rule 4: Implied; Tier 2 and unverified; does not decide K0 or K1.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: not searched (shared search limit reached).

rows.branch: religious and lay Taoism chiefly; philosophical readers often set it aside
rows.reference: Taishang Ganying Pian 太上感應篇, list of wicked deeds
rows.original: 賞及非義，刑及無辜；殺人取財，傾人取位；誅降戮服，貶正排賢
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project (Legge 1891, SBE 40, not displayed for these lines)
rows.says: Among the deeds for which the recording spirits shorten a person's life: rewarding the undeserving and punishing the innocent; killing people to take their property; overthrowing people to take their posts; killing those who have surrendered and slaughtering those who have submitted; and pushing aside the upright.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K0's 'for your own gain' limb (殺人取財) and Explicit for K3's 'those who have surrendered' (誅降戮服). 'Punishing the innocent' is a court matter (context, rule 5). Tier 2, not counted: reported beside the labels (rule 1).

rows.reference: Taishang Ganying Pian, closing section on retribution; and list of wicked deeds
rows.original: 枉殺人者，是易刀兵而相殺也 ... 損子墮胎
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Lead from memory: whoever wrongly (枉) kills people is in effect trading weapons so that they will be killed in turn. The list of wicked deeds also includes harming children and causing abortion.

rows.reference: Lingbao Ten Precepts (十戒); Five Precepts of Lord Lao (老君五戒); Hundred and Eighty Precepts Spoken by Lord Lao (老君說一百八十戒)
rows.original: 一者不殺 (lead)
rows.says: Lead from memory: the first precept in the Five and Ten Precepts is not to kill, extended in the Lingbao version to all living beings. The Hundred and Eighty Precepts include rules against killing and injuring.
rows.bearing: If confirmed, a wider rule (no killing of any living being) that would teach K1 and K0 for the religious branches (rule 7). No precept text was found that permits killing. Unverified and not counted: does not decide.

rows.branch: early religious Taoism (Taiping Jing, in the Daozang)
rows.reference: Taiping Jing 太平經, passage on killing girls
rows.original: 殺女 (lead)
rows.says: Lead from memory: condemns the practice of despising and killing baby girls as a sign that the world has lost the Way.
rows.bearing: Would speak directly to newborns (rule 9) and against a status-based exception for girls. Outside the corpus and unverified: does not decide.

counter.reconciliation:
No counted text (Tao Te Ching; Zhuangzi in Guo Xiang's 33 chapters) was found that permits, commands or approves a private person's killing of someone who is not attacking, that allows killing newborns or children, that makes a killing blameless because of the victim's status, or that limits protection to one's own community. The hard texts are images (Tao Te Ching 5), satire and reports (Zhuangzi 8, 10, 29), a presupposed practice used as an image (Zhuangzi 19 on revenge), perspectivist passages (Zhuangzi 2 and 6), or texts on rulers' punishments and war (Tao Te Ching 30, 31, 74; Zhuangzi 4, 6, 11, 24, 25). So there is little for the tradition to reconcile on the floor itself; what needs reconciling is how some lines read. The tradition does this as follows.
1. Its own counted texts (Tier 1, every branch). Chapter 5's 'straw dogs' is answered in the same book: the sage casts away no one (27, verified), is good to the not-good (49, verified) and harms no one (60, verified, with a re-check on ctext pending). Chapter 62 ('if a person is not good, why cast them away?') would make this explicit for wrongdoers but is unverified. Chapter 63 (answer injury with kindness, verified) excludes revenge; a modern conjecture (Yan Lingfeng, Chen Guying; unverified) would move the phrase to 79, but the received texts of both classical commentators keep it in 63. Chapter 74 warns that whoever kills in place of the one who presides over killing cuts his own hands (verified only on a site not on the project's list). In the Zhuangzi, the parables of Hundun (ch. 7) and the seabird (ch. 18) teach against imposing on others, and ch. 4 says whoever brings calamity on others will meet it (verified in Article I research).
2. Classical commentators (Tier 2, used for reconciliation; the standard traditional readings named in corpus.md). Heshang Gong (transmitted within religious Taoism) and Wang Bi read 不仁 in chapter 5 as impartial non-interference, not cruelty. This is reported in R. Wagner (2003); Wang Bi's clause 天地任自然，無為無造 was seen in this pass only in an unattributed quotation, so the reading is unverified on a project site. Heshang Gong reads 司殺者 in chapter 74 as Heaven (unverified). Guo Xiang and Cheng Xuanying on Zhuangzi 10, 19, 25 and 29 were not checked.
3. Literati criticism (outside the corpus; standing: an influential scholar's judgment, not a Taoist religious authority). Su Shi (1037 to 1101), in his Record of the Shrine Hall of Zhuangzi, held chapters 28 to 31 (including Robber Zhi and the sword-fight) to be later additions (unverified). The chapters remain in the canonical text, and nothing in them approves killing in any case.
4. Religious Taoism (Tier 2, not counted). The Treatise on Response and Retribution names as life-shortening wrongs killing people for their property, killing those who have surrendered or submitted, and punishing the innocent (verified on zh.wikisource). It also condemns wrongful killing and harming children (unverified). The precept texts reportedly put 'do not kill' first (unverified). The Taiping Jing (outside the corpus) reportedly condemns killing baby girls (unverified).
5. The Liezi (Tier 2, flagged) reports the killing of firstborn sons among a foreign people and says such customs are not to be thought strange. This is the nearest thing to a hard text on newborns. It is a report used to show that customs vary, it is not counted, and it is unverified in the Liezi itself; only a parallel in the Taiping Guangji (citing the Bowuzhi and Mozi) was seen. Mozi, outside the tradition, tells the same story to condemn it.
No statement by a modern Taoist body (for example the Chinese Taoist Association) was searched for. One honest limit: the counted texts teach against killing mainly through the example of the sage, who is often the ruler. A plain rule 'do not kill', addressed to every private person and naming newborns, appears only in Tier 2 and in precept texts. That is why K1 and K0 are borderline rather than firm.

K1.label: Taught (borderline); not contradicted
K1.reason: Rule 7: Tao Te Ching 27, 49 and 60 (Tier 1, every branch; verified by search) teach through the sage's example that no one is cast away, that the not-good are treated with goodness, and that the sage harms no one. This is a wider rule that reaches everyone K1 protects, including wrongdoers, at the Clear teaching level. It is borderline, as in Article I, because it describes the sage (often the ruler) rather than stating a rule for every private person, and no counted text names newborns or private killing directly (rule 9; the Liezi report on firstborn sons is Tier 2, flagged, unverified and only a report). Not contradicted: the hard texts are images or reports (Tao Te Ching 5; Zhuangzi 2, 8, 10, 19, 29; rule 4) or concern rulers' punishments and war (Tao Te Ching 74; Zhuangzi 4, 6, 11, 25; rule 5). No counted text found lets a master, parent, husband, kinsman, crowd or religious leader kill, or grades protection by status. Tier 2 support (the Ganying Pian, verified) is reported beside the label (rule 1).

K0.label: Taught (borderline); not contradicted
K0.reason: Rule 7: Tao Te Ching 63 (answer injury with kindness; verified) teaches against revenge at the Clear teaching level, and the same wider rule as K1 (27, 49, 60) covers killing for gain or from anger. Borderline on the same grounds as K1, and because a modern conjecture moves 63's phrase to chapter 79 (unverified; the classical texts keep it in 63). Tao Te Ching 31 (whoever delights in killing cannot win the world) would add Clear teaching but is unverified. No counted text approves revenge or killing for gain: Zhuangzi 19 only presupposes revenge (rule 4), and Zhuangzi 25 calls revenge the conduct of a common man. The Ganying Pian's explicit 'killing people to take their property' (verified) is Tier 2 and not counted (rule 1).

K3.label: Silent in counted texts (Implied only); taught explicitly in Tier 2 only
K3.reason: Rule 8 with rule 1: the counted texts teach restraint in war in general, but no verified counted text names non-combatants, children, the old or those who surrender. Tao Te Ching 30 and 31 (mourn the many killed, stop once the aim is achieved) are unverified. Zhuangzi 24 (no side is good when one kills another state's soldiers and people for land) is unverified for that line, Zhuangzi 25 mocks war, and Zhuangzi 28 is unverified: all are Implied for K3. Only the Ganying Pian (Tier 2, not counted; verified) explicitly condemns killing those who have surrendered or submitted (誅降戮服). No Taoist text was found that approves killing non-combatants.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 60
rows.original: 非其神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人
rows.translation: James Legge, The Tao Teh King, SBE 39 (1891)
rows.says: Ruling a large state is like cooking small fish. When the world is ruled by the Tao, the spirits do not harm people, and neither does the sage (Legge adds 'ruling'). Neither side harms the other. It describes good rule; it is not worded as an order.
rows.bearing: A wider duty not to harm people (rule 7). Nothing limits who is protected, so it includes K1 and K0. This is the main counted basis, read with rows 2 to 4. Borderline: it describes the sage, here as ruler, and does not name killing or private persons. Same basis as Article I row 7b.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 49 (received text; the Mawangdui manuscript reads 聖人恆無心)
rows.original: 善者，吾善之；不善者，吾亦善之 ... 聖人皆孩之

rows.bearing: Sets the reach of the wider duty: it covers the not-good, so 'the wicked' are included (rule 7). It does not name killing, so on its own it is Implied for K1; read with row 1 it is part of the Clear teaching, borderline (as Article I row 7a).

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 74
rows.original: 若使民常畏死，而為奇者，吾得執而殺之，孰敢？常有司殺者殺。夫代司殺者殺，是謂代大匠斲
rows.says: Threatening death is useless if people do not fear it. If they did, and wrongdoers could be seized and put to death, who would dare? But there is always One who presides over killing; whoever kills in his place is like someone hewing wood for the master carpenter, and seldom escapes cutting his own hands. Legge's note: the chapter sets out the inefficiency of capital punishment and warns rulers against it.
rows.bearing: A ruler's punishment, so context only (rule 5). It presupposes judicial killing and warns against taking killing into one's own hands. By a fortiori argument it gives no warrant to a private person, but it does not say so: Implied for K1. It permits no private killing, so it does not contradict (rule 2).

verified.reconciliation:
No counted text (Tao Te Ching; Zhuangzi in Guo Xiang's 33 chapters) was found that does any of the following: permits, commands or approves a deliberate killing by a private person or by the head of a household or community; lets newborns, children, servants, strangers or 'the wicked' be killed; or makes a killing blameless because of who the victim is. So no contradicting counted text needs reconciling. The hard texts fall into four groups, and the tradition handles each in its own terms.

(1) Rulers' punishment: Tao Te Ching 74 (verified); Zhuangzi 4, 6 (以刑為體), 11 and 25 (unverified). These are context only (rule 5). Tao Te Ching 74 itself warns that whoever kills in place of 'the One who presides over killing' cuts his own hands. Heshang Gong, the classical commentary that corpus.md names for reconciliation and that is transmitted within religious Taoism, reads that One as Heaven (verified through Legge's note). Legge reads the chapter as warning rulers against capital punishment.

(2) War: Tao Te Ching 31 (verified); 30, 68 and 69 (unverified); Zhuangzi 24, 25 and 28 (partly verified). Weapons are used only when unavoidable, delight in killing is condemned, and the dead are mourned. These are context for K1 and K0, and Implied for K3.

(3) Images, satire and reports: Tao Te Ching 5; Zhuangzi 2, 6, 8, 10, 14, 19, 29 and 30; Liezi 5. Reporting is not approving (rule 4).
- Tao Te Ching 5's 'straw dogs' is answered in the same book: the sage harms no one (60), casts away no one (27), is good to the not-good (49), and the Tao does not abandon them (62). Wang Bi and Heshang Gong reportedly read 不仁 as impartial non-interference (unverified).
- Zhuangzi 19 uses blood revenge only as an image.
- Zhuangzi 25 calls revenge the conduct of a common man.
- Zhuangzi 14 (unverified) presents 'killing a robber is not killing a man' as a mark of decline.
- Su Shi (outside the corpus, unverified) judged chapters 28 to 31 to be later additions.

(4) Newborns: no counted text speaks of them. The only nearby report is a custom of eating firstborn sons. It is attributed to Liezi 5 (Tier 2, flagged) but was found only in the Bowuzhi. It is told to show that customs differ, and Mozi tells the same story to condemn it.

Religious Taoism's later texts make the line explicit. The Ganying Pian (Tier 2, verified) lists killing people for their wealth, unjust killing, and killing those who have surrendered among wrongs that shorten life. The precept texts reportedly put 'do not kill' first (unverified).

The one structural limit is unresolved. The counted texts teach non-harm through the sage, often the ruler. No classical commentary (Heshang Gong or Wang Bi on 49 and 60; Guo Xiang on the Zhuangzi) was checked on whether that duty binds every private person. Article I treated the sage as the model for everyone. The same reading is used here, which is why the results are marked borderline.

K1.label: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule
K1.reason:
Rule 7. Tao Te Ching 60 says the sage does not harm people (Tier 1, every branch, VERIFIED (search)). This is a wider duty not to harm, and it includes not killing. Tao Te Ching 49 (good to the not-good) and 27 (casts away no one) set its reach to everyone, 'the wicked' included; 62 and 81 support it (Implied). This is the same basis on which Article I counted Taoism.

It is borderline for three reasons:
1. The lines describe the sage, often as ruler, and are not worded as rules for every private person.
2. No counted text names killing, private persons or newborns. Newborns are covered only through the general word 'people' (rule 9).
3. The classical commentaries were not checked on whether the sage's non-harm binds private persons.

Rules 2 and 3 are not met. No counted text permits a private, household or crowd killing, or grades protection by faith, status, sex or age.
- Tao Te Ching 74 and Zhuangzi 6 concern rulers' punishment, and Tao Te Ching 31 concerns war: context only (rule 5).
- Zhuangzi 19 (revenge as an image), 29 and 10 (robbers), 14 (status exception shown as decline; unverified) and Tao Te Ching 5 are reports or images (rule 4).
- The Liezi report on firstborn sons is Tier 2, flagged, unverified in the Liezi, and only a report.

Rule 6 does not apply. No counted text bearing directly on K1 has a disputed meaning. The disputed 殺其殺 in Zhuangzi 14 sits inside a report of decline and is unverified.

If the project lead holds that the sage-ruler's non-harm does not bind private persons, the label falls to Silent (rule 8), not Contradicted.

The counted rows were confirmed against recorded search output and earlier project records, not fresh searches. Direct reading is needed before admission. The Ganying Pian's explicit lines are Tier 2 and are reported beside the label (rule 1).

K0.label: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule, with Clear teaching against revenge
K0.reason:
K0 is narrower than K1, so the same wider duty covers it (Tao Te Ching 60 with 49 and 27; rule 7).

Tao Te Ching 63 (recompense injury with kindness; VERIFIED (search)) is Clear teaching against revenge. It does not name killing, and a modern conjecture that moves the phrase to ch. 79 is unverified; the received texts keep it in 63. The 'gain', 'anger' and 'hatred' clauses rest on the wider rule alone. Tao Te Ching 46 and 68 would strengthen them but are unverified. Tao Te Ching 31's condemnation of delight in killing is set in war (context).

It is borderline on the same grounds as K1.

No counted text approves killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge:
- Zhuangzi 19 only presupposes revenge (rule 4).
- Zhuangzi 25 calls revenge a common man's conduct.
- Zhuangzi 28's ruler gives up land rather than have people killed (context, Implied).

The Ganying Pian is Explicit against killing people for their wealth (VERIFIED (search)) but is Tier 2 and does not decide (rule 1).

K3.label: Not contradicted; silent in counted texts (Implied only)
K3.reason:
Rule 8 with rule 1. Tao Te Ching 31 (VERIFIED (search)) limits all killing in war: only when unavoidable, without delight, and mourned with funeral rites. But it does not single out children, the old, civilians or those who have surrendered, so it is Implied.
- Tao Te Ching 30 and 69 are unverified.
- Zhuangzi 24's line on killing another state's people is unverified.
- Zhuangzi 25 mocks war.
- Zhuangzi 28 shows a ruler sparing his people's lives (Implied).
No counted text approves killing non-combatants. Only the Ganying Pian (Tier 2, not counted, VERIFIED (search)) explicitly condemns killing those who have surrendered or submitted.

Parity caveat: in this round, the secular humanism check counted a general non-harm clause as reaching non-combatants. It reasoned that the tradition accepts war only as defence against attackers, so people who are not fighting stay protected. Applied to Taoism, the same reasoning would join Tao Te Ching 60 (the sage harms no one) with 31 (arms only when unavoidable) and give 'Taught (wider rule), borderline'. The project lead should decide once, for every tradition, whether a general non-harm rule reaches conduct in war, and then apply the decision to both.

verified.branch_notes:
The counted texts are accepted across Taoism:
- the Tao Te Ching, read by philosophical readers and held as revealed scripture by the religious orders;
- the Zhuangzi, honoured as the Nanhua zhenjing (from knowledge; not checked).

So the K1, K0 and K3 results do not differ by branch on counted texts.

Under METHOD decision 3, the living branches are probably Zhengyi (including the Celestial Masters and Lingbao lineages) and Quanzhen. 'Philosophical Taoism' is a readership rather than a community with its own body of texts. This is not yet decided in corpus.md.

Tier 2 texts divide by branch:
- The Ganying Pian is used in religious and lay practice; philosophical readers often set it aside.
- The Hundred and Eighty Precepts belong to the Celestial Masters lineage.
- The Lingbao Ten Precepts are now used within Zhengyi ordination.
- The Initial Perfection Ten Precepts are Quanzhen's own.
- The Liezi is scripture for religious Taoism and widely read by others.

All the precept texts are unverified. If corpus.md were to treat them as primary for the religious branches (decision 4), and they were verified, each branch would probably have Explicit teaching for K1 through its own precepts. That would not change the whole-tradition result, which already rests on texts every branch accepts.

Not checked:
- the Xiang'er commentary (the Celestial Masters' own reading of the Tao Te Ching, outside the corpus);
- Guo Xiang and Cheng Xuanying on any Zhuangzi passage;
- statements by modern bodies such as the China Taoist Association.
verified.fairness_notes:
1. Teaching style. The 'borderline' mark comes from who the duty falls on (the sage, often the ruler), not from Taoism teaching through sayings. Article I treated the sage as the model for every follower (note 6), and the same reading is used here. An adherent may still feel that rule-based traditions get 'taught' without qualification while Taoism always carries 'borderline'. The project should state once that the sage's conduct is read as the tradition's model for everyone, or else apply the same caution to other traditions whose ethics are framed as the ideal person's conduct (for example the Confucian junzi or the Stoic sage).

2. K3 parity. As set out under K3, the secular humanism check let a general non-harm clause reach non-combatants in war. Taoism's verified Tao Te Ching 60 plus 31 would support the same result. Labelling Taoism 'silent' while humanism is 'taught' on comparable evidence would be a different standard.

3. Precept texts. Religious Taoists treat their ordination precepts as binding, and several are presented as scripture revealed by Lord Lao or the Heavenly Worthy (titled 經). The project counts the Sunnah for Sunni Islam, the Talmud for Rabbinic Judaism and ʿAbdu'l-Bahá's writings as primary. Decision 4 should be applied to the Taoist precept texts by the same test, and their status decided, before any 'silent' result for the religious branches is reported as final.

4. Narrative and satire. The Zhuangzi's robbers, assassins and sword-fights are reported speech and satire. They must be read under rule 4, exactly as narrative passages in the Hebrew Bible, the Mahabharata or Buddhist Jatakas are.

5. The newborn report. The firstborn custom was found only in the Bowuzhi. There it reads 'not to be thought wrong'; the version attributed to the Liezi reads 'not to be thought strange'. Presenting either as Taoist teaching would be unfair. It is a report of foreign customs, its place in the Liezi is unconfirmed, the Liezi is flagged Tier 2, and Mozi tells the same story to condemn it.

6. Translation. Tao Te Ching 5 looks harsher in modern versions that render 不仁 as 'ruthless'. The project uses Legge ('not benevolent'), as translations.md says. Tao Te Ching 81 was seen only in an unidentified non-Legge translation.

7. Verification. This verifier made no new searches. Every check was made against the researchers' recorded search output and earlier project records, as was done for secular humanism in this round. The same direct-reading requirement applies before admission.
